newsitem.title: UK: Tiny Albania has the seeds for more Balkan trouble.
newsitem.headline: Tiny Albania has the seeds for more Balkan trouble.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Tiny, impoverished Albania is virtually ignored by the West, but violent upheavals on the streets there could contain the seeds of yet more trouble for the unsettled Balkans.
Diplomats and analysts say unrest in Albania, which has already claimed three lives, might affect ethnic Albanians living in the Kosovo region of Serbia and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
These are already highly sensitive areas, with unresolved ethnic and minority problems despite the end of the war in former Yugoslavia.
Fresh problems there could draw in Greece, sensitive about its relations with Macedonia, and then Turkey -- dragging two NATO allies who are already at each other's throats into a potential conflict.
"There is a certain domino effect that one could see, which worries some people," said one Western diplomat, who asked not to be identified.
"At the moment, the problems in Albania are internal questions, they are about poverty and the rule of law. But they may not remain so."
"Albania is in a key position," said Christopher Cviic, an authority on the former Yugoslavia.
"It could mean the spread of instability in the region, ultimately affecting things in Serbia and between Greece and Turkey."
During the war in former Yugoslavia, the United States took the threat of unrest in Kosovo very seriously for these reasons, warning Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic not to stir trouble there.
Kosovo was the initial focus for Milosevic's brand of nationalism which promised to protect and unite the Serbs. It drove Yugoslavia to collapse and war.
The overwhelming majority of people in Kosovo, around 90 percent, are ethnic Albanians. Milosevic removed freedoms and a degree of autonomy they had enjoyed in 1989, accusing them of separatism.
With Milosevic now under pressure from mass protests in Belgrade and elsewhere, there has also been more more recent trouble in Kosovo.
Last week, Albania denounced Belgrade's crackdown on dissent after Serb police killed three ethnic Albanians in the province's main city, Pristina. There were also dozens of arrests.

Diplomats said there are some fears the Albanian government might take a more aggressive stance on Kosovo, perhaps as a way of distracting people at home from their grinding poverty and political grievances.
"If you put that together with Milosevic's problems, you can see why there is so much concern," said another Western envoy.
In Macedonia, there is a sizeable ethnic Albanian minority -- and similar resentment about cultural and linguistic rights.
Partly because of fierce arguments with Greece about cultural heritage and because of the Albanian question, Macedonia has also been seen as a likely tinderbox by Western powers.
The United States and Nordic countries deployed troops there as part of a small U.N. peacekeeping force in 1992, as a preventive measure to stop the conflict spreading from the rest of Yugoslavia.

Greece is already highly sensitive about its neighbours because of the current tension with Turkey over Cyprus and other issues. Diplomats say fresh problems in Macedonia would make the situation worse.
Critics say the West has spent too much time and effort on countries like Poland and Hungary that will soon join NATO or the European Union, and not enough on the more obscure parts of the Balkans.
Albania, with a population of just over three million, existed in almost total isolation as a Stalinist state for years.

Few people outside know much about it, although the same could be said for Sarajevo before the war in Bosnia -- or before the political assassination in the Bosnian capital that set off World War One in 1914.
"One needs to pay attention to the Balkans when things are not quiet there," said Cviic.
"Neglect can be very expensive."
